title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night nine: auto-rickshaws wear garlands, a mechanic puts a flower on his wrench, and the last name in the list is the giver of accomplishment

segments.voice: Yesterday was night eight of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Mahagauri, and girls served first at the table. Whom did you serve? Tonight is the last night, and the end of the goddess's part of the year. Day one thousand one hundred seventeen.
screen: `SEE THE BRIGHTNESS IN A CHILD.` · `NIGHT NINE.`

segments.voice: An auto-rickshaw parked outside a temple, with a garland of marigolds across its windshield and a smear of turmeric on the bumper. A mechanic's shop where the wrenches have been wiped clean, laid in a row and given a flower each. A tailor's sewing machine with a red dot on it. A laptop, closed, with a sprig of something green on the lid. In parts of South India, the ninth day of Navaratri is Ayudha Puja, the worship of tools. Where it's kept, the tools aren't worked with today. They're cleaned, thanked and honored. And the ninth name in the Kavacha's list, the last one, is Siddhidatri.
screen: `A GARLAND ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `A FLOWER ON EACH WRENCH.` → `THE LAST NAME: SIDDHIDATRI.`

segments.voice: Siddhidatri is called the giver of siddhi, of accomplishment, the power to bring a thing to completion. On this night she's shown seated on a lotus, calm, the end of the list. It's fitting that the curriculum's last night is about finishing. Look back over the nine nights. In the three-by-three way of keeping them, Durga's nights cleared the road, Lakshmi's nights filled the house, and Saraswati's nights turned toward knowing. In the nine forms, the goddess was a daughter of the mountain, a smile that made a world, a mother with her child, a warrior named for a sage's hermitage, night itself, the bright one washed clean. And now she gives accomplishment. Ayudha Puja says where accomplishment actually comes from: the work of your hands, and the tools you do it with. The wrench, the sewing machine, the pen, the stove. Honoring them for a day says the ordinary instruments of a life are worth bowing to. And remember night one. Near the end of the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess herself speaks of the great worship offered to her in autumn, and says that whoever hears her story then, with devotion, will be freed from troubles by her grace. So the curriculum ends where it began, bound to the book. That's where this part of the year closes. It began with the Devi Mahatmya read whole. Then the goddesses as characters, Shakti as a philosophy, the Sri Sukta, the names of Lalita, and these nine nights. Tomorrow the year turns to Shiva, and to the Shiva Purana.
screen: `SIDDHIDATRI, GIVER OF ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `CLEAR, FILL, KNOW, FINISH.` · `HONOR THE TOOLS OF YOUR HANDS.` · `THE AUTUMN WORSHIP AND THE BOOK.` · then, large: `THE GODDESS'S PART, COMPLETE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: thank your tools. Settle, and let the breath slow. One by one, bring to mind the things your hands use to get through a day. Keys. A phone. A pan. A pen, a keyboard, a steering wheel, a broom. Don't rush. Let each one come up, and give it a moment of thanks, the way the mechanic gives each wrench a flower. Then let the hands themselves come to mind, resting in your lap. They're tools too. If you pray, you can offer the work of your hands to the goddess, or to God, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night nine: Siddhidatri, the giver of accomplishment, and the day the tools rest and are honored.

Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Today, clean one tool you use every day, slowly, and put it back where it belongs. Day one thousand one hundred seventeen. The goddess's part, complete.
